title: The Election of 1828 and the Right to Vote
summary: See how each state's electors voted in 1828, then turn on who could vote there: the property and tax rules for white men, and whether free Black men could vote. Students test the idea that Jackson's election was a victory for the common man against the rules state by state.
subject: History
time: About 60 minutes, or two parts: questions 1 to 4, then 5, 6 and the big question
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

map.about: This map shows the presidential election of 1828 in the 24 states of that year. A pie on each state shows how its electors voted, for Andrew Jackson or John Quincy Adams, with bigger pies for more electors. Two layers, off when the map opens, show who could vote in each state: whether white men had to own property or pay a tax, and whether free Black men could vote. Each state's pop-up gives the votes, how its electors were chosen, the rules and their sources.

layers.name: Election of 1828: electors' votes
layers.shows: A pie on each of the 24 states: electors' votes for Andrew Jackson (blue) and John Quincy Adams (orange), with bigger pies for more electors. The pop-up gives the votes, who chose the electors and both voting rules, with sources.
layers.source: National Archives (Electoral College results, 1828); state outlines from Natural Earth

layers.name: Free Black men and the vote, 1828
layers.shows: Each state shaded gray by whether free Black men could vote: light gray, could vote on the same terms as white men; middle gray, only with extra rules or kept out in practice; dark gray, could not vote. Off when the map opens.
layers.source: State constitutions and laws, as cited in each pop-up

layers.name: White men and the vote, 1828
layers.shows: Each state shaded gray by its rule for white men: light gray, no property or tax rule; middle gray, had to pay a tax or meet a similar rule (militia service, road work or a little land); dark gray, had to own property. Off when the map opens.
layers.source: State constitutions and laws, as cited in each pop-up

knownIssues.note: Some rules rest on historians' accounts rather than the law's own text, or sources differ; the pop-up says so (North Carolina's rule for electors, Rhode Island's 1822 law, Louisiana's and Missouri's clauses, how Illinois and Missouri chose electors).
The names come from today's basemap: a few are under pies, and the basemap also names places that were territories in 1828 (Michigan, Arkansas, Florida). Clicking a state gives its name.
Quotes the 1785 law's own words, "free negroes or mulattoes", as a primary source. Teacher notes say so.

compellingQuestion.en: Andrew Jackson's election in 1828 is often called a victory for the common man. Who could vote in 1828, and did it depend on where you lived?

questions.task: With only the votes layer on, find which states voted for Jackson and which for Adams, and the states that split.
frontOfClass: Open The 24 states of 1828 bookmark.
Open the legend: blue is Andrew Jackson, orange is John Quincy Adams, and bigger pies mean more electors.
Ask: which part of the country voted mostly for Adams, and which for Jackson?
Click the pie on New York and read the votes.
Ask: which states split their electors between the two?

steps.en: Open The 24 states of 1828 bookmark and open the legend.
Find the blue pies (Andrew Jackson) and the orange pies (John Quincy Adams).
Click the two-color pies and read the votes in each pop-up.

ask.en: (a) Which part of the country voted mostly for Adams? (b) Which part voted mostly for Jackson? (c) Which three states split their electors?

answer.where: Election of 1828: electors' votes layer, legend and pop-ups. All orange: Connecticut, Delaware, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Vermont. All blue: the South and the West (Alabama, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia) and Pennsylvania. Split: New York (Jackson 20, Adams 16), Maryland (Jackson 5, Adams 6) and Maine (Jackson 1, Adams 8).
answer.accept: (a) New England and nearby states (New Jersey, Delaware). (b) The South and the West (except Delaware and most of Maryland), plus Pennsylvania. (c) New York, Maryland and Maine.
answer.text: Totals, not on the map: Jackson 178, Adams 83 (National Archives).

questions.task: Before turning on the voting-rule layers, students predict where white men had to own property or pay a tax to vote, and where free Black men could vote, with a reason. They write the prediction down first.
frontOfClass: Keep only Election of 1828: electors' votes on.
Ask: in which states do you think white men still had to own property or pay a tax to vote? Older states on the coast, or newer states in the West?
Ask: where do you think free Black men could vote? Have students write their predictions before anyone turns on a layer.

steps.en: Keep only Election of 1828: electors' votes on.
Look at which states are old (on the Atlantic coast) and which are newer (west of the Appalachian Mountains).
Write your predictions before you turn on any other layer.

ask.en: (a) Where do you think white men still had to own property or pay a tax to vote? (b) Where do you think free Black men could vote? Give a reason for each.

answer.accept: Any prediction with a reason, for example that the older coastal states kept older rules, or that newer western states were more open. Predictions are checked in questions 3 and 4, not marked right or wrong here.

questions.task: Turn on White men and the vote, 1828 and compare the shading with the prediction and with the votes.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn on White men and the vote, 1828.
Scroll down the legend to the key: light gray is no property or tax rule, middle gray is pay a tax (or a similar rule), dark gray is own property.
Ask: which two states are dark? Open the New England and New York bookmark to find Rhode Island.
Ask: where are the light states, and did Jackson win only in states with no rule?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn on White men and the vote, 1828.
Scroll down the legend to its key: light gray means no property or tax rule, middle gray means pay a tax (or a similar rule), dark gray means own property.
Click a dark state and a light state and read White men in each pop-up. Rhode Island is small: use the New England and New York bookmark.

ask.en: (a) Which two states are shaded dark? (b) Where are the light states (no rule)? (c) Did Jackson win only in states with no rule? Was your prediction right?

answer.where: White men and the vote, 1828 layer. Dark (had to own property): Virginia and Rhode Island. Light (no rule): Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, New York, Maryland, Kentucky, Tennessee, Indiana, Illinois, Alabama and Missouri, and South Carolina for state elections. Middle (pay a tax): Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, North Carolina, Georgia, Ohio, Mississippi and Louisiana.
answer.accept: (a) Virginia and Rhode Island; also accept North Carolina with the reason that its state Senate voters needed 50 acres. (b) About half are newer states west of the Appalachian Mountains (Kentucky, Tennessee, Indiana, Illinois, Alabama, Missouri); the others are Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont and New York in the North, and Maryland and South Carolina. (c) No: Jackson won Virginia, where white men had to own property, and several tax states; Adams won states with no rule (Vermont, New Hampshire, most of Maine and Maryland) as well as Rhode Island. The rules and the result don't line up neatly.
answer.text: New York's 1821 constitution eased the rules for white men and an 1826 amendment removed what was left. Virginia's property rule was loosened by a new constitution in 1830. Delaware's and South Carolina's rules were for state elections: their legislatures chose the electors. In South Carolina and Tennessee a man could qualify by owning land or by living in the area six months, so no property was needed.

questions.task: Turn off the white men layer and turn on Free Black men and the vote, 1828; compare with question 3.
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn off White men and the vote, 1828 and turn on Free Black men and the vote, 1828.
Scroll down the legend to the key: light gray is could vote, middle gray is only with extra rules or kept out in practice, dark gray is could not vote.
Ask: in which states could free Black men vote on the same terms as white men?
Open the New England and New York bookmark and click New York. Read White men and Free Black men.
Ask: Indiana, Illinois, Alabama and Missouri had no property or tax rule for white men. What does this layer show for free Black men there?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn off White men and the vote, 1828 and turn on Free Black men and the vote, 1828.
Scroll down the legend to its key and find the light gray states (could vote).
Open the New England and New York bookmark, click New York and read White men and Free Black men.

ask.en: (a) Name the states where free Black men could vote on the same terms as white men. (b) How were New York's rules for white men and for Black men different? (c) Indiana, Illinois, Alabama and Missouri had no property or tax rule for white men. What does this layer show for free Black men there?

answer.where: Free Black men and the vote, 1828 layer and pop-ups. Light gray (could vote on the same terms): Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, North Carolina (until 1835) and Tennessee (until 1834). Middle gray: New York (the 1821 constitution set a new rule for Black men only: own property worth $250, pay tax on it and have been a citizen for three years) and Pennsylvania (the law didn't mention race, but in many places officials kept Black men from voting). Dark gray (could not vote): the other 16 states.
answer.accept: (a) Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, North Carolina and Tennessee. (b) White men in New York had no property or tax rule after 1826, but Black men had to own $250 of property. (c) All four shut out free Black men: in these states voting was opened to more white men while Black men were kept out. Tennessee, also west of the Appalachians, is the exception: free Black men could vote there until 1834.
answer.text: In 1825 only 298 Black men in the whole state of New York met the $250 rule (Peter J. Galie, Albany Law Review, citing Phyllis Field; Galie gives nearly 6,000 free adult Black New Yorkers). Before 1821 New York's property rules were the same for all voters. Free Black men lost the vote in North Carolina in 1835 and in Tennessee under its 1834 constitution.

questions.task: Read the pop-ups for South Carolina and Delaware (the legislature chose electors) and Georgia (voters chose them for the first time); explain what "expanded suffrage" meant in 1828, and for whom.
frontOfClass: Click South Carolina and read Who chose the electors. Then open The Middle Atlantic bookmark and click Delaware.
Ask: did voters in these states choose the president's electors?
Click Georgia and read Who chose the electors.
Ask: what changed in Georgia in 1828?
Ask: by 1828, who had gained the right to vote, and who had not?

steps.en: Click South Carolina and read Who chose the electors. Then open The Middle Atlantic bookmark and click Delaware.
Click Georgia and read Who chose the electors.

ask.en: (a) Who chose the electors in South Carolina and Delaware? (b) What changed in Georgia in 1828? (c) Textbooks say suffrage expanded in the Age of Jackson. Using the map, who had gained the right to vote by 1828, and who had not?

answer.where: Pop-ups. South Carolina and Delaware: the state legislature chose the electors, so voters had no direct say. Georgia: voters chose the electors for the first time (the legislature chose in 1824); Louisiana's and Vermont's pop-ups say the same.
answer.accept: (a) The state legislature. (b) Voters chose the electors for the first time. (c) More white men could vote: the property rules had gone in many states (for example New York in 1826, Massachusetts in 1821), and in Georgia, Louisiana and Vermont voters chose the electors for the first time. But women could vote nowhere, free Black men could vote on the same terms as white men in only six states, and in two states voters didn't choose the electors. Students may add, from what they know, that enslaved people could not vote.
answer.text: Every pop-up says: "Women could not vote in any state in 1828." New Jersey had ended women's voting in 1807.

questions.task: Students ask what the map can and can't show: it shows the rules in law, not who actually voted.
frontOfClass: Click Pennsylvania and read Free Black men.
Ask: what is the difference between what the law said and what happened?
Ask: what would you need, besides this map, to know how many people actually voted in 1828?

steps.en: Click Pennsylvania and read Free Black men.
Read the sentence about women at the end of any pop-up.

ask.en: (a) In Pennsylvania, how was what happened different from what the law said? (b) Which people does the map not show? (c) What else would you need to find out how many people actually voted in 1828?

answer.where: Pennsylvania pop-up: the constitution didn't mention race, but in many places, Philadelphia among them, officials kept Black men from voting; a new constitution shut them out in 1838. Every pop-up: women could not vote in any state in 1828.
answer.accept: (a) The law allowed Black men to vote, but officials kept many from voting. (b) Enslaved people, and people in the territories, who couldn't vote for president; women appear only in the note that they could not vote. (c) Popular vote counts by state, newspapers, poll records or diaries: the map shows the rules, not who turned out.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from all three layers and at least two pop-ups, then write one "why" question the map raised. Accept answers that say who could vote depended on the state, name the property states (Virginia and Rhode Island) and the tax states, note that free Black men could vote on the same terms as white men in only six states and women in none, and weigh the 'common man' description: more white men could vote, and many people could not.

student.en: Answer the big question, Andrew Jackson's election in 1828 is often called a victory for the common man. Who could vote in 1828, and did it depend on where you lived?, using evidence from all three layers and at least two pop-ups. Then write one "why" question this map raises for you.

objectives: Describe the result of the 1828 election by region using the pies, legend and pop-ups.
Make and test a prediction about where white men had to own property or pay a tax to vote.
Compare the rules for white men and for free Black men in the same states, including New York.
Explain what expanded suffrage meant in 1828 and for whom, using evidence from the pop-ups.
Distinguish what the law said from what happened, using Pennsylvania as an example.
discussion: Your predictions in question 2: what did you base them on, and what surprised you?
New York removed the property rule for white men but kept one for Black men. Why might a state do both at once?
Is 'a victory for the common man' a fair way to describe 1828? Who would agree, and who might not?

differentiation.support: Do questions 1, 3 and 4 from the front with the legend open, and give pairs a list of the six states where free Black men could vote on the same terms as white men to check on the map.
differentiation.stretch: Open the source link in New York's pop-up, find the 1822 version of the voting clause, and find the words that set the $250 rule; compare them with the rule for white men.

resources.title: New York Constitution of 1821 and the 1826 amendment
Constitution of North Carolina, 1776 (Arts. VII and VIII)
Voting Rights in New Jersey before the 15th and 19th Amendments

assessment.evidence: Strong answers use the pies (Adams in New England, Jackson in the South and West, three split states), the white men layer (Virginia and Rhode Island property, the tax states, the light states), the free Black men layer (six states, New York's $250 rule) and the pop-ups' note on women.
assessment.exemplar: Who could vote in 1828 depended a lot on where you lived. In the votes layer, Adams won New England and Jackson won the South and the West, but the voting rules don't follow that split. When I turned on the white men layer, Virginia and Rhode Island were dark gray, so a white man there had to own property, while in Indiana, Illinois and Alabama there was no property or tax rule. Jackson won Virginia anyway. The free Black men layer showed that free Black men could vote on the same terms as white men in only six states, and Indiana, Illinois, Alabama and Missouri shut them out. New York's pop-up says white men had no property rule after 1826, but Black men had to own $250 of property. Every pop-up also says women could not vote in any state. So 1828 was a victory for more white men, but not for everyone the common man might include.

beforeYouStart.en: In 1828, Americans did not vote for the president directly. Each state chose electors, and the electors voted for president. Andrew Jackson ran against President John Quincy Adams. Each state made its own rules about who could vote. Some states made men own land or pay a tax to vote. Suffrage means the right to vote. A legislature is a state's lawmakers. The militia was a state's citizen soldiers.

readingTheMap.en: Blue pies: electors for Andrew Jackson. Orange pies: John Quincy Adams. Bigger pies mean more electors. Only the pies are on at the start; turn on the other layers in Map layers when a question asks. In both rule layers, light gray means fewer limits and dark gray means more. The key for the gray layers is lower down in the legend: scroll to see it. Click a state to read its votes, its rules and the sources; scroll to see all of the pop-up.

reflection.en: Turning on the rules one layer at a time, what did you notice about who could vote that a list of election results would not show?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: The map opens with only Election of 1828: electors' votes on. Students turn on White men and the vote, 1828 in question 3 and Free Black men and the vote, 1828 in question 4; question 2's prediction works best before those layers are on. State names come from today's basemap: a few are under pies, and some named places were territories in 1828; clicking a state gives its name. Small states are easier to click with the New England and New York and The Middle Atlantic bookmarks. Jackson's supporters presented him as a champion of ordinary people, and many textbooks describe 1828 as a victory for the common man; the lesson tests that description. Virginia's pop-up quotes the 1785 law's own words, "free negroes or mulattoes", as a primary source; you may want to say so before students read it.

misconceptions.claim: In 1828 every white man could vote.
misconceptions.response: Virginia and Rhode Island still required property, and ten states required a tax or a similar rule (militia service, road work or a little land).

misconceptions.claim: Jackson won because the states with the most open rules voted for him.
misconceptions.response: The map doesn't show that: Jackson won Virginia, a property state, and Adams won states with no property or tax rule.

misconceptions.claim: Voters chose the electors in every state.
misconceptions.response: In South Carolina and Delaware the state legislature chose them.

misconceptions.claim: If the law allowed it, people could vote.
misconceptions.response: In Pennsylvania the law didn't mention race, but officials kept many Black men from voting.

standards.text: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
Explain specific roles played by citizens (such as voters, jurors, taxpayers, members of the armed forces, petitioners, protesters, and office-holders).
Explain the impact of the election of Andrew Jackson, including expanded suffrage
Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
